findings.title: The asserted n^(2/3) breakdown contradicts the actual MLE limit
findings.source_heading: ## Issue 2019__accepted__v20-18-314__I01 — The asserted n^(2/3) breakdown contradicts the actual MLE limit
findings.markdown:
**Exact location:** PDF 8, Section 3.2, Theorems 2–3; PDF 28, Appendix B.3, Eqs. (42)–(49), especially Eq. (49); PDF 30, radial contradiction; PDF 31–32, Appendix B.4; PDF 14, discussion.

**Claim:** Under global-null logistic regression with uniform scaled Stiefel design or nonsingular Gaussian design, marginal MLE normality in Eq. (11) fails at p asymptotic to n^(2/3), giving an exact asymptotic p-value breakdown threshold.

**Error and evidence:** The claimed radial contradiction does not follow from marginal normality. For the exact sequence p=floor(n^(2/3)) under both stated designs, the MLE is finite and unique with probability tending to 1, and sqrt(n)betahat_j/2 converges to N(0,1). The corresponding Eq. (11) and observed-information Wald p-values remain asymptotically uniform.

Let p=floor(n^(2/3)), y_i iid Bernoulli(1/2), independently of X. Take either X=G with iid N(0,1) entries, or X=sqrt(n)G(G'G)^(-1/2), which is exactly the theorem's uniform scaled Stiefel design. The true parameter is 0. These satisfy the two theorems' complete design/null hypotheses; no sparsity or additional conditions are imposed in their statements.

Write w(t)=exp(t)/(1+exp(t))², g=X'(y−1/2), and H(beta)=X'diag(w(Xbeta))X, the Hessian of negative unnormalized log likelihood. We prove that for each fixed j, sqrt(n)betahat_j/2 converges to N(0,1), contradicting the asserted failure at p~n^(2/3). The argument also proves ordinary observed-information Wald p-values converge to Uniform(0,1).

## A uniform small-subset bound

For each m-row subset S, take 1/4-nets of the unit spheres in R^m and R^p, of sizes at most 9^m and 9^p. The bilinear net inequality gives ||G_S||op≤2max_{u,v in nets}|u'G_S v|. Each fixed net pair is a standard scalar Gaussian, with tail at most 2exp(−a²/2). There are at most (en/m)^m row subsets. Taking a²=2[m log(en/m)+(m+p)log9+3logn] and a union bound gives, with probability≥1−2n^(−3),
sup_{|S|≤m}||G_S||op²≤C[p+m log(en/m)+logn].
Sets smaller than m can be padded. Constants are absolute. This union bound accounts for data-dependent row selection.

Also ||G'G/n−I||op→0 in probability since p/n→0. Explicitly, for a fixed unit v,||Gv||²~chi²_n and P(|chi²_n/n−1|>t)≤2exp(−nt²/8) for 0<t<1. A 1/4-net of size 9^p and the quadratic-form net inequality ||E||op≤2max_net|v'Ev| yield the claim on taking t²=16(p log9+3logn)/n. In the Stiefel representation ||X_S||op≤sqrt(n)||G_S||op/smin(G)=(1+op(1))||G_S||op. Therefore the same subset bound applies to either design, and ||X'X/n−I||op→0 (exactly 0 for Stiefel).

Set R_n=16sqrt(p/n), delta_n=n^(−1/24), and m_n=ceil(512p n^(1/12)), which is O(n^(3/4)) and eventually<n. Uniformly for ||beta||≤R_n, on ||X||op²≤2n the bad set S_beta={i:|x_i'beta|>delta_n} has
|S_beta|≤||Xbeta||²/delta_n²≤2nR_n²/delta_n²≤m_n.
Since m_n log(en/m_n)/n→0 and p/n→0, the preceding subset bound gives
sup_{||beta||≤R_n}||X_{S_beta}||op²/n=o_p(1).

## Uniform Hessian approximation and MLE existence

The scalar inequality 0≤1/4−w(t)≤C delta_n² holds when |t|≤delta_n, while 0≤1/4−w(t)≤1/4 globally. Consequently, as PSD matrices,
0≤H(0)−H(beta)≤C delta_n² X'X+(1/4)X_{S_beta}'X_{S_beta}.
Hence
sup_{||beta||≤R_n}||H(beta)/n−I/4||op=o_p(1).
This includes all points along every segment from 0 inside the ball, without assuming that beta is independent ofX.

For GaussianX, g is exactlyN(0,nI/4) unconditionally, by conditioning on the Rademacher label vector, whose norm issqrt(n)/2. For StiefelX,
||g||²=(n²/4)B, with B~Beta(p/2,(n−p)/2), so ||g||/(sqrt(np)/2)→1. Thus||g||≤sqrt(np) with probability→1 in either case.

The negative log likelihood L has gradient−g at 0. On the uniform-Hessian event H(beta)≥(n/8)I within the ball, for ||beta||=R_n,
beta'gradL(beta)=beta'[int_0^1 H(tbeta)dt]beta−beta'g
≥(n/8)R_n²−R_n||g||≥32p−16p=16p>0.
Every boundary point can therefore be improved by an inward move. The continuous convex objective has an interior minimizer on the compact ball, whose gradient is 0. SinceX has full column rank and w(t)>0 at every finite t, L is strictly convex; this is the unique global finite MLE. Existence probability tends to1, avoiding separation issues. On the vanishing failure event define the estimator 0; this keeps rotational equivariance and does not affect convergence.

## Spherical remainder gives the coordinatewise CLT

The score equation and uniform Hessian approximation yield
g=[int_0^1 H(tbetahat)dt]betahat,
betahat=4g/n+e_n,
||e_n||=o_p(sqrt(p/n)).
Both design laws are invariant underX→XQ for every fixed orthogonalQ; labels are independent and unchanged. The unique MLE and g transform as Q'betahat andQ'g. Thus their difference e_n has a spherical distribution. A spherical random vector has a uniform direction U_p independent of its radius, and sqrt(p)U_{p,j}=O_p(1). It follows that
sqrt(n)e_{n,j}=[||e_n||/sqrt(p/n)]sqrt(p)U_{p,j}=o_p(1).

For GaussianX,2g_j/sqrt(n) is exactlyN(0,1) unconditionally. For HaarX the conditional Rademacher sum2g_j/sqrt(n)=sum_i(x_ij/sqrt(n))(2y_i−1) has variance1 and satisfies the Lindeberg condition because max_i|x_ij|/sqrt(n)→0 in probability. Hence
sqrt(n)betahat_j/2=2g_j/sqrt(n)+o_p(1) converges to N(0,1).

This holds even under the conditional-in-probability interpretation: jointP(|sqrt(n)e_j|>epsilon)→0 implies P(|sqrt(n)e_j|>epsilon|X)→0 in probability overX by Markov. The conditional score CLT holds for designs with maximal normalized coordinate→0. For GaussianX the conditional variance||x_j||²/n→1 as well. The normalizations in Eq11 are exactlysqrt(n)/2 for Stiefel and asymptotically equivalent for GaussianI because A=X'X/4. Moreover H(betahat)/n→I/4 in operator norm, so observed-information Wald normalization also has this limit.

## Why the printed contradiction fails

PDF 28 Eq. 42–49 assumes marginal CLT, then makes it an exact growing-dimensional Gaussian independent ofX. Neither implication follows. Let Z_p~N(0,I), independent ofX, and B_n=(2/sqrt(n))(1+p/n)Z_p. **Exact location:** PDF 13, Corollary 5.1 and its first proof equality; PDF 12, transfer from fixed-tau risk to optimal horseshoe; PDF 2 and PDF 4 Section 1.4.1, central contribution statements.

**Claim:** For every true orthogonalized coefficient vector alpha, the horseshoe estimator with global tau selected by minimizing its fixed-tau SURE has prediction risk no greater than the horseshoe posterior mean with fixed tau=1.

**Error and evidence:** Fixed-tau SURE unbiasedness cannot be applied after selecting tau from the same data. The actual tuned horseshoe differs on an open region from the unique Bayes rule under the proper tau=1 horseshoe prior. An exact conditional squared-loss identity makes its integrated risk strictly larger, contradicting the claimed inequality for every alpha.

Take n=3, p=6, sigma²=1 and X=[I3 I3]/sqrt(2). Then XX'=I3, so all three singular values equal 1, exactly the D=I assumption in Section 5. With W=X' and beta=W alpha, the orthogonalized observation is Y=alpha+epsilon, epsilon~N(0,I3). An independent future observation adds the same irreducible risk 3 to every estimator.

Write delta_tau(Y) for the paper's horseshoe posterior mean at fixed tau. Put the paper's proper product horseshoe prior on alpha at tau=1: independent lambda_i~half-Cauchy, alpha_i|lambda_i~N(0,lambda_i²). Let m be its prior predictive density, which is positive everywhere. Despite the prior's infinite variance, T=alpha−Y=−epsilon is square integrable. Thus delta_1(Y)=Y+E(T|Y) has integrated estimation risk E||T−E(T|Y)||²≤3. The conditional squared-loss projection identity gives, for any rule a with finite integrated risk,

    integral [R(alpha,a)−R(alpha,delta_1)] Pi(dalpha)
      = E_m ||a(Y)−delta_1(Y)||².

This also holds for prediction risk because the additional future-noise constant cancels. If a differs from delta_1 on a set of positive m-probability, the right side is strictly positive. It cannot therefore have risk at most that of delta_1 for every alpha. If its integrated risk is infinite, the claimed dominance is already impossible.

It remains to verify that the actual SURE selector differs, with genuine finite interior minimizers rather than a boundary ambiguity. For s=y²/2 and theta=tau^(−2), let m_k=E(Z^k) under the paper's exact density

    q_tau(z) proportional to (1−z)^(−1/2) exp(−sz)
                             / [theta+(1−theta)z],  0<z<1.

The fixed-tau scalar prediction SURE is

    S_tau(y)=2[1−m_1+2s m_2−s m_1²].

At y=0,tau=1, Z~Beta(1,1/2), so S_1(0)=2/3 and its tau derivative equals 16/45. At tau=1 the derivative for a general y is exactly

    S'_1(y)=4 Var(Z)−8s Cov(Z²,Z)+8s m_1 Var(Z).

At the explicit three-dimensional observation Y=(6,0,0), exact rational bounds certify

    S_1(Y)<3.6<6<36,       S'_1(Y)>0.6>0.

Here 36 is the limit of S_tau(Y) as tau tends to zero, and 6 is its limit as tau tends to infinity. These follow directly from the density concentrating respectively at Z=1 and Z=0. Since the tau=1 value is strictly below both endpoint limits, the global SURE minimum is attained in a compact subinterval of (0,infinity). Every minimizer differs from 1 because the derivative there is nonzero. Continuity gives the same strict conditions on an open neighborhood U of (6,0,0).

The rational certification is reproducible without numerical integration. At s=18,tau=1, substitute z=1−u² and define

    J_k = integral_0^1 (1−u²)^k exp(18u²)du,
    m_k = J_k/J_0.

The exact positive series is

    J_k = sum_{j>=0} (18^j/j!) * 2^k k!
                    / product_{r=0}^k (2j+2r+1).

Sum j=0,...,80 with rational arithmetic. Every integral coefficient is between 0 and 1, so the entire remaining tail is at most (18^81/81!)/(1−18/82). Propagating these rational intervals through the displayed formulas proves S_1(Y)<18/5 and S'_1(Y)>3/5. Full exact numerator/denominator bounds are saved in the evidence JSON. The decimal centers are approximately 3.5753502269308344 and 0.6416563020162883; the proof uses rational comparisons.

For nonzero y the posterior mean delta_tau(y)=y[1−E_tau(Z)] varies strictly with tau. Indeed, with W(Z)=(1−Z)/[theta+(1−theta)Z],

    d E_tau(Z)/d tau = (2theta/tau) Cov(Z,W(Z)) < 0,

since W is strictly decreasing and Z is nondegenerate. The first coordinate is nonzero throughout a sufficiently small U. Therefore every SURE minimizer there produces an estimate different from delta_1. Because m(U)>0, the squared-distance expectation in the Bayes identity is strictly positive.

Apply this identity to the actual SURE-tuned rule. Corollary 5.1 would make the integrated risk difference nonpositive for every alpha; the identity makes it strictly positive. This directly contradicts its universal quantifier. The argument permits any measurable completion outside U if the unrestricted argmin fails to exist for some other data. Allowing endpoints or changing tie conventions cannot repair the contradiction on U. It is an exact integrated contradiction, not a claim to have identified a particular alpha by Monte Carlo.

The failed proof step is the first equality on PDF 13: fixed-tau SURE is unbiased for delta_tau, but substitution of tauhat(Y) does not preserve that identity. Where differentiable, the divergence of the composite estimator also contains sum_i (partial delta_tau,i/partial tau)(partial tauhat/partial Y_i); discontinuous selection can add further effects. Independence of the sampling law from a fixed tuning constant does not make a selected constant independent of the observations.

**Reason for rejection:** The paper explicitly identifies Theorem 5.1 and Corollary 5.1 as its specific finite-sample prediction-risk contribution (PDF 2), and describes comparisons with tuning parameters chosen to optimize SURE as a main theoretical result (PDF 4). The false corollary is the bridge transferring fixed-tau calculations to the actual tuned estimator used in the simulations. Selection-aware risk analysis or a different procedure is required; a local constant, fixed-tau formula correction or boundary convention cannot restore this impossible uniform dominance. The correct fixed-tau SURE tools, some fixed-tau gains and empirical comparisons do not establish the advertised tuned risk guarantee. This warrants rejection of the paper as written.

**Discovery method:** While tracing the fixed-tau SURE formulas into the fitted-estimator risk comparison, noticed that the first equality in Corollary 5.1 omits the effect of data-dependent tuning. Tested the claim using the fixed horseshoe posterior mean’s own proper prior.

**Verification method:** Read all 39 pages, Appendix A.1–A.6 and the included supplement; inspected the original rendered claim and centrality statements. Derived the exact proper-prior projection contradiction for the original horseshoe family, proved attained interior SURE minima differ from tau=1 on an open region, and certified an explicit data point using rational exponential-series bounds. Fixed-tau numerical controls and independent bounded original-PDF/mathematical QA pass.

**Confidence:** High. The contradiction uses the original estimator and a legal full-row-rank design, with an explicit finite data point certified by exact rational arithmetic. A square-integrable noise projection handles the horseshoe prior’s infinite variance. Independent original-PDF and mathematical QA confirms the argument and centrality. No simulation-based universal inference or historical ranking reversal is asserted.

 Correct fixed-tau formulas pass independent controls; the null fixed-tau prediction risk is approximately 1.23824496523, below the paper’s 1.75 bound. Original simulation/real-data drivers, splits and tuning grids were not located, and no published empirical ranking is claimed false.

findings.title: Prior-draw partitions and likelihood-only weights converge to the wrong posterior
findings.source_heading: ## Issue 2019__accepted__v20-18-374__I01 — Prior-draw partitions and likelihood-only weights converge to the wrong posterior
findings.markdown:
**Exact location.** PDF page5, Eqs1–2 (Gaussian-mixture input model and GP experts); page6, first three paragraphs and Algorithm1; page7, Section3.2, proposal construction and importance ratio; page8, opening asymptotic-unbiased claim and Eq3. Page7 calls the generated partitions approximate samples; this finding does not claim that approximation was undisclosed.

**Claim.** The method draws input-mixture parameters from their prior and assigns each input by its normalized mixture responsibilities. It treats those partitions as draws from `p(Z|X)` and, in Eq3/Algorithm1, weights them only by `L_Z=p(Y|X,Z)`. Page6 claims an exact inference algorithm when the generating model is an MOE, and page8 claims an asymptotically unbiased estimate of posterior expectations `E[g(f)]`. The displayed NIW/Dirichlet model imposes no restriction that would make prior mixture parameters independent of the observed inputs after conditioning.

**Error and evidence.** Write `phi=(pi,mu,v)` for the input-mixture parameters. The specified procedure samples from

`q(Z|X)=integral p(phi) p(Z|X,phi) dphi`,

whereas the model's conditional partition law is

`p(Z|X)=integral p(phi|X) p(Z|X,phi) dphi`.

The cancellation in Eq3 uses the second density although the sampler uses the first. With likelihood-only weights, the normalized large-J limit is proportional to `q(Z|X)L_Z`, instead of `p(Z|X)L_Z`. This is a fixed approximation error, not the acknowledged finite-J self-normalization bias. A concrete proper NIW example demonstrates that it affects the latent GP posterior itself.

Take one input dimension, two clusters, `N=B=2`, `X=(-6,6)`, `Y=(0,0)`. Set `a=alpha=1000000`, `b=a-1`, independently

- `pi ~ Dirichlet(alpha,alpha)`;
- `v_k ~ InverseGamma(a,b)`, with density proportional to `v^(-a-1) exp(-b/v)`;
- `mu_k|v_k ~ N(0,v_k)`.

This is Eq1's proper one-dimensional NIW prior with `mu0=0`, `lambda=1`, `nu=2a`, `Psi=2b`. All variances are positive, and `alpha>1` meets the balanced-cluster design discussion. Use known GP amplitude1, observation-noise variance1 and squared-exponential lengthscale `12/sqrt(2 log2)`, giving correlation `rho=k(-6,6)=1/2`. `pi1 in[.49,.51], v1,v2 in[.99,1.01], mu1,mu2 in[-.25,.25]`.

Each conditional mean condition therefore has probability greater than.19. The event probability is greater than `.99*.97*.19^2`. For either input, its absolute conditional assignment log odds are at most

`log(.51/.49)+.5log(1.01/.99)+6.25^2/(2*.99)-5.75^2/(2*1.01)`

`=3.4109667...<3.5<log40`.

For a singleton at either input, `b_1=b+9`; for both inputs together, `b_2=b+36`. Hence

`m_2(-6,6)/m_1(-6)^2=(2/sqrt3)*[Gamma(a+1)Gamma(a)/Gamma(a+.5)^2]`

`* (1+9/b)^(2a+1)/(1+36/b)^(a+1)`.

`E=(2a+1)*9/b-(a+1)*(36/b-648/b^2)`

`=-222214333325/12345654321<-17.99`.

`((alpha+1)/alpha)*(4/sqrt3)*(4/sqrt15)*exp(E)`

`=3.63475687105e-8<1e-7`.

This strict upper bound alone proves a discrepancy of orders of magnitude; independent65-digit conjugate evaluation gives the true probability `1.81723162737e-8`.

Finally choose the posterior functional `g(f)=f(-6)f(6)`. With S, Gaussian conditioning gives latent crosscovariance `rho/(4-rho^2)=2/15`; with different clusters it is zero. Conditional means are zero in both cases. The correct posterior expectation is therefore below `4.8463425e-9`. In contrast, the algorithm's likelihood weighting increases its actual proposal's same-cluster probability because `4/sqrt15>1`. Its estimator consequently converges to a crossmoment greater than

`(2/15)*(3466683/2101250000)=1155561/5253125000=.0002199759...`.

Investigated whether normalized pointwise responsibilities could nevertheless have the correct integrated partition law.

**Verification method.** Read the entire journal PDF and rechecked original rendered pages6–9 and all definitions. Derived the actual proposal and the conjugate true partition law; constructed a proper NIW/Dirichlet/RBF example; certified the event lower bound and posterior upper bound analytically with exact rational exponent arithmetic, and transferred the discrepancy to a latent GP functional. Retrieved and Git-SHA-verified the cited source both at its last prepublication commit and its current commit; no hidden conditional-parameter draw resolves the written method.

Source commits are `7d1b2a98022067873f42f1c77fff52541398ebc6` (2019-01-17, prepublication) and `cc1f5cf430abc85c98bdb02549ba3d9fd7ea134c` (2022-04-12). findings.title: The main PLAIS solver does not perform descent and can diverge on the scalar Gaussian problem
findings.source_heading: ## Issue 2019__accepted__v20-18-483__I01 — The main PLAIS solver does not perform descent and can diverge on the scalar Gaussian problem
findings.markdown:
**Exact location.** PDF p.16, Section 5.1, the claim that PLAIS-Impute solves the collective completion program and inherits the fast `O(1/T²)` convergence rate; PDF p.17, Algorithm 4, especially line 9 and the argument passed to Approx-SVT in line 12. Compare the required proximal argument in PDF p.14, equations (9) and (11), and PDF p.15, Algorithm 1 and the displayed negative-log-likelihood gradient. The released implementation linked on PDF p.16 has the corresponding failure in `solver/PLAIS-Impute/PLAISImpute.m`, lines 67 and 76–78, and `powerMethodAccMatComp.m`. Equation (4), whose minimizer the solver is supposed to compute, is on PDF p.8.

**Claim.** The paper presents PLAIS-Impute as its main efficient algorithm for the nuclear norm penalized negative-log-likelihood problem (4), and states that it shares the accelerated `O(1/T²)` convergence rate. With step size one, the proximal argument must be `Q − ∇L(Q)`, as the paper itself correctly gives in equations (9)/(11) and Algorithm 1. The scalar Gaussian likelihood is a special case of the stated model, has globally Lipschitz gradient with constant one, and requires no approximate singular-subspace calculation.

**Error and evidence.** Algorithm 4 instead writes `Z = ∇L(Q)` and passes that gradient alone to SVT. This is not repaired by the linked implementation: it adds the negative-log-likelihood gradient, using `Q + ∇L(Q)`, rather than subtracting it. `LikelihoodAndGradLikelihood.m` returns the actual negative-log-likelihood gradient, including its leading minus sign; this is not a convention in which a positive-gradient update would descend.

Take one observed Gaussian entry `y = 1/2`, known variance one, `γ = 1`, and `λ = 1/100`. There are no missing entries or heterogeneous-block ambiguities. Dropping the irrelevant likelihood constant, equation (4) becomes

\[
\min_{|w|\le1} F(w),\qquad
F(w)=\tfrac12 w^2-\tfrac12 w+\tfrac1{100}|w|.
\]

Its unique minimizer is the interior point `w* = 49/100`, and `∇L(w) = w − 1/2`. All Gaussian curvature/domain requirements are satisfied. At `w = 1/4`, the released update, with momentum reset, is exactly

\[
\operatorname{soft}_{.01}(w+\nabla L(w))
=\operatorname{soft}_{.01}(0)=0.
\]

The objective rises from `F(1/4) = −73/800 = −0.09125` to `F(0) = 0`. The correct minus-gradient update gives `soft_.01(1/2) = .49` and the exact minimum `F(.49) = −2401/20000 = −0.12005`.

The failure is sustained rather than an isolated accelerated nonmonotonic step. Calling the unchanged released full solver with

```matlab
para = struct('decay', .01, 'maxR', 1, 'maxIter', 25, 'tol', 1e-6);
[U,S,V,out] = PLAISImpute(.5, .01, para, {{'gaussian',[.5,1]}}, 1, 1);
w = U*S*V';
```

returns approximately `w = −397324.4970066158`. The reported objective grows from about `−.117661` at iteration 1 to `7.8933580596 × 10^10` at iteration 25. The final continuation parameter is `.01`. Rank is one throughout, so this cannot be explained by an inaccurate truncated SVD. The restart is present and executes; after it resets the momentum, the erroneous update still points away from the optimum. In the negative half-line, with zero momentum, it has the form `w_next = 2w − .5 + λ_t`, with `λ_t < .015`; it continues moving away from the minimizer.

The literal printed Algorithm 4 also fails independently of the source-code sign. From its prescribed scalar initialization `w0 = w1 = .5`, `λ0 = .5` and decay `.01`, its gradient-only SVT gives `w2 = 0`, then approximately `−.489951`, `−.97995051`, and `−1.4699505051`. Once negative, the restart leaves `Q = w` and the gradient-only rule decreases `w` by more than `.485` per step. Thus neither the printed main algorithm nor the released algorithm has the asserted convergence behavior. The correct proximal map is available in Algorithm 1, but it is not the map used in Algorithm 4 or in this implementation.

**Reason for rejection.** This invalidates a principal computational contribution: the paper's main proposed solver is not an accelerated optimizer for its stated convex program, and can diverge even in a full-rank one-entry Gaussian case with an interior solution. The computational bridge from the statistical estimator to the reported recovery experiments is therefore unsupported as written. Replacing the solver map and checking the approximate-power and restart steps, then rerunning the recovery study, is necessary before the algorithmic convergence and empirical corroboration can be accepted. A correction to the printed line alone does not establish those results because the linked executable method also uses the wrong direction. This finding does **not** assert that the ideal penalized estimator's statistical theorems are false, or that a corrected implementation must reverse the published ranking.

**Discovery method.** While tracing the implementation of equation (4) through the gradient definition, approximate power method, and experimental drivers, I noticed that the solver added the returned negative-log-likelihood gradient. Comparing this with the original rendered algorithm also exposed the gradient-only printed argument.

**Verification method.** Read all 43 PDF pages, including Appendices A–C, and inspected the rendered equations/algorithms on pp.8 and 14–17. Authenticated all 186 files in the authors' prepublication repository at commit `e62a49b3674d6983f00eb676e87afbcbd54e59dc` (25 September 2019) against Git blob hashes. Ran the unchanged authored likelihood, optimizer, power, and SVT functions under Octave 10.3. The only runtime adapter replaces the platform-specific `partXY` MEX dot-product loop by the same explicit scalar products. An independent reviewer reran the full scalar solver and obtained the divergence above; exact rational arithmetic verifies the objective values and the printed Algorithm 4 trajectory. Ninety scalar controls confirm that the correct minus-gradient update returns the exact Gaussian minimizer.

The source experiment drivers invoke this solver. Vector-path checks also match all 12 recovery curves in the archived `relative_errors.pdf` to published Figure 3 within `0.000024` PDF point, and all six rank curves to Figure 2. Those matches authenticate the plotted artifacts, but do not prove the archived solver generated the archived tables. The original seeds and latent matrices were not recovered. The archived Figure 4 bars differ from the final paper, and one Figure 1 curve does not match at the same tolerance. No historical corrected score, ranking reversal, or complete figure rerun is claimed.

**Reproducible evidence files.** an unpublished audit file, `collective483-gentile-qa.py`, and `collective483-math.py`; results and logs under unpublished audit files, especially `native-controls.json`, `gentile-bounded-qa.json`, `gentile-native-gaussian.log`, `mathematical-controls.json`, `source-manifest.json`, and `figure-provenance.json`.

**Confidence: High.** The objective and its unique minimizer are exact, the sign and published algorithm were rechecked against the original PDF and authenticated source, and independent unchanged-body native runs reproduce sustained divergence in a scalar case. The rejection rationale rests on this false central solver/convergence claim, with the historical empirical-attribution limits stated explicitly.

findings.title: The central empirical-Bayes E-step has no posterior in the dimensions used for the leukemia analysis
findings.source_heading: ## Issue 2019__accepted__v20-18-484__I01 — The central empirical-Bayes E-step has no posterior in the dimensions used for the leukemia analysis
findings.markdown:
**Exact location.** PDF pp.6–7, Section 3.1, the independent Jeffreys priors, claimed inverse-Wishart conditional posterior, Algorithm 1 E-step, and the “Initialization and Convergence” argument asserting a continuous bounded marginal likelihood. PDF p.21, Section 6 and footnote 1, specifies shared dimension `s = 45` and group sizes `(15,27,64,20,43,79,79)`. The released `subspace-functions.R`, function `subspaceEM`, provides an additional check of the attempted numerical repair.

**Claim.** The paper estimates the shared subspace by maximum marginal likelihood using EM. It assumes independent priors

\[
p(M_k)\propto|M_k|^{-(s+1)/2},\qquad p(\sigma_k^2)\propto1/\sigma_k^2,
\]

asserts that `M_k | V` is inverse-Wishart with scale `VᵀS_kV` and degrees of freedom `n_k`, and uses

\[
E[M_k^{-1}\mid V]=n_k(V^TS_kV)^{-1}
\]

in its main EM algorithm. It then applies that procedure at `s = 45`, including groups with fewer than 45 observations. The paper's convergence argument says that compactness of the Stiefel manifold and continuity make the marginal likelihood bounded.

**Error and evidence.** If `n_k < s`, then

\[
\operatorname{rank}(V^TS_kV)
\le\operatorname{rank}(S_k)
\le n_k<s
\]

for **every** `p × s` orthonormal `V`. Thus the matrix inverse in the asserted E-step does not exist anywhere on its parameter space. More fundamentally, the asserted conditional posterior is not a probability distribution. A generalized inverse cannot supply the expectation of a nonnormalizable posterior.

Here is an explicit positive-volume divergence argument. Take `n = 2`, `p = 5`, `s = 3`, data rows `e₁ + e₄` and `e₂ + e₅`, and `V = [e₁,e₂,e₃]`. The projected scatter is `A = diag(1,1,0)`, while the residual scatter is 2, so the noise variance has positive residual information. This is a legal finite data matrix for the Gaussian model; the same rank obstruction holds for every data matrix with `n < s`, including after centering. The construction can be embedded in larger feature dimensions.

In precision coordinates `T = M⁻¹`, the posterior kernel asserted by the paper becomes

\[
|T|^{(n-s-1)/2}\exp[-\operatorname{tr}(AT)/2].
\]

Parameterize positive-definite `T` by

\[
T=\begin{pmatrix}H&b\\b^T&t+b^TH^{-1}b\end{pmatrix},
\quad H\succ0,\ t>0,\ b\in\mathbb R^2.
\]

Then `det(T) = det(H)t`, `tr(AT) = tr(H)`, and the change from the last diagonal entry to `t` has Jacobian one. This density is independent of `b`. Even restricting `H` and `t` to compact positive sets, its integral over all `b ∈ R²` is infinite. Consequently neither the claimed inverse-Wishart posterior nor its expected precision exists.

This directly applies to the paper's clinical example: `s = 45` exceeds several reported group sizes. Removing sample means lowers the scatter rank further. Footnote 1 caps the later group spike rank `r` at `min(n_k,s)` for the conditional Gibbs stage; it does not change the 45-dimensional matrix in the EM E-step. Appendices A–C supply no alternative prior, valid singular-posterior model, or different E-step for this case.

The source's small ridge does not establish the claimed procedure. The authenticated prepublication code replaces the printed expected precision by

\[
(n_k+s+1)(V^TS_kV+10^{-5}I)^{-1}
\]

and uses noise precision `[n_k(p−s)+2]/R_k(V)`, where `R_k(V) = tr((I−VVᵀ)S_k)`. These are not the paper's E-step coefficients. The first expression can be interpreted as an expected precision under a different proper inverse-Wishart prior, or as an inverse posterior-mode calculation with a ridge; neither interpretation is the asserted Jeffreys EM derivation.

Even regularizing the `M` prior leaves a separate zero-noise-scale divergence. For data rows `e₁,e₂`, use

\[
V_\theta=[\cos\theta\,e_1+\sin\theta\,e_4,e_2,e_3],\quad \theta>0.
\]

The residual scatter is `R(Vθ) = sin²θ > 0`, and projected scatter is `diag(cos²θ,1,0)`. Under a proper inverse-Wishart ridge prior with scale `εI`, its integrated `M` factor tends to a finite positive constant as `θ → 0`. The independent noise integral is proportional to `R(Vθ)⁻²` under the printed Jeffreys prior, or `R(Vθ)⁻³` under the noise-shape interpretation of the source's `+2` numerator. Both diverge. Thus this is a sequence of positive-residual subspaces, not merely evaluation at one singular boundary point. The source E-step returns noise precisions about `602`, `60002`, `6000002`, `600000004`, then infinity as `θ = .1,.01,.001,.0001,0`, despite its finite `M` ridge. For any group with `s ≥ rank(S_k)`, a subspace can contain its entire sample row space, giving the same noise-collapse mechanism.

The covariance interpretation `M = σ²(Ψ+I)` does not supply the missing remedy. Enforcing `Ψ ⪰ 0`, hence `M ⪰ σ²I`, couples/truncates the parameter support; the conditional distributions would no longer be the independent unrestricted inverse-Wishart and inverse-gamma distributions asserted in the paper. That would require a different derivation and inference algorithm.

**Reason for rejection.** This affects the central empirical-Bayes construction, rather than an auxiliary bound or isolated numerical edge case. Under the dimensions actually used in the headline application, its stated E-step has no posterior expectation for any candidate subspace. Its maximum marginal likelihood and boundedness justification therefore cannot support that analysis as written. A restriction `s < n_k` would exclude the reported 45-dimensional clinical application. Replacing the priors/support and deriving a well-defined inference objective, including a remedy for zero residual variance, changes the central estimation procedure and requires reanalysis; the existing numerical ridge alone does not do this. A finite locally initialized numerical output is not an EM estimate of the nonexistent asserted posterior. This finding does not claim that all possible shared-subspace models are invalid or that particular biological conclusions must reverse.

**Discovery method.** While tracing the claimed inverse-Wishart E-step into the leukemia application, I compared the selected shared dimension with the group sample sizes and noticed that its projected scatter must be singular.

**Verification method.** Read all 37 PDF pages, including Appendices A–C, and rechecked the rendered priors, Algorithm 1, application dimensions and footnote. Derived the rank obstruction, explicit precision-coordinate nonnormalizability proof and positive-residual marginal-divergence sequence. Authenticated all 25 source blobs at the authors' May 20, 2019 commit `ec91b12e6b7fa898729ff130181eec24ed83ead8`; inspected the actual regularization and conditional formulas. Executed the unchanged authored E-step with a no-op M-step adapter solely to capture its precision values along the exact sequence. An independent reviewer checked the original PDF and posterior-propriety argument. No historical fitted clinical objects or complete clinical rerun were recovered, and no empirical ranking reversal is claimed.

**Confidence: High.** The rank deficiency holds deterministically for every sample in the stated dimensions, and an explicit positive-volume integral proves nonnormalizability. The original PDF, clinical dimensions, source formulas and native E-step checks agree; no missing-artifact inference is needed for the central failure.

findings.title: Gaussian chained learning retains unit total variance instead of becoming strongly self-sustaining
findings.source_heading: ## Issue 2019__accepted__v20-18-539__I01 — Gaussian chained learning retains unit total variance instead of becoming strongly self-sustaining
findings.markdown:
**Exact location.** PDF page10, Section3.5: the shared-h sampling paragraph, Eq17, the definition of strong epsilon-self-sustainability, and the variance recurrence in Eq18. PDF page11, Theorem3 and the variance part of its proof. The model's shared-h sampling is also explicit on PDF page4, Section3.

**Claim.** In Gaussian chained learning, learner t first draws one hypothesis h from learner t-1's posterior and then receives m_t independent N(h,sigma^2) measurements conditional on that h. Each learner uses the common prior N(bar_mu,bar_sigma^2); learner0's posterior is N(mu0,sigma0^2). Theorem3 asserts that, for any 0<epsilon<1 and arbitrarily small c>0, the displayed schedule

`m_t=(|mu0-bar_mu|/epsilon)*(1+1/c)*(sigma/bar_sigma)^2*t^(1+c)`

makes learning strongly epsilon-self-sustaining. By the explicit definition on page10, this requires both bounded mean bias and `sigma_t^2+Var(mu_t)→0`, with variance taken over the learning randomness. All parameters in the counterexample below satisfy this model with strictly positive variances.

**Error and evidence.** The measurements in a session are independent conditional on their common teacher hypothesis. They remain correlated after that hypothesis is integrated out. Eq18 omits the covariance terms and incorrectly divides the inherited uncertainty by m_t.

Write

`beta_t=m_t*bar_sigma^2/(sigma^2+m_t*bar_sigma^2)`,
`r_t=Var(mu_t)`, and `V_t=r_t+sigma_t^2`.

With independent standard normals Z_t,E_t, the specified sampling and Eq17 give the exact representation

`H_t=mu_(t-1)+sigma_(t-1)*Z_t`,
`mu_t=(1-beta_t)*bar_mu+beta_t*(H_t+sigma*E_t/sqrt(m_t))`,
`sigma_t^2=bar_sigma^2*(1-beta_t)`.

Here H_t is the one teacher hypothesis shared by the session. Therefore

`r_t=beta_t^2*(V_(t-1)+sigma^2/m_t)`.

Combining this with the posterior variance and the identity `beta_t*sigma^2/m_t=bar_sigma^2*(1-beta_t)` yields

`V_t=beta_t^2*V_(t-1)+bar_sigma^2*(1-beta_t^2)`.

This differs from the printed Eq18, which uses `beta_t^2/m_t` to multiply the inherited variance. Equivalently, the omitted covariance is `Cov(d_(t,i),d_(t,j))=V_(t-1)` for distinct observations i,j in the same session.

Take the legal Gaussian parameters

`mu0=1, bar_mu=0, sigma0^2=bar_sigma^2=sigma^2=1`.

The exact recursion then gives `V_t=1` for every t by induction, for **any** positive session lengths. Thus the total variance cannot tend to zero, regardless of how rapidly the lengths grow. For a completely integer-valued instance of the theorem's own schedule, take epsilon=1/2 and c=1, giving `m_t=4t^2`. Then explicitly

`sigma_t^2=1/(1+4t^2)`,
`Var(mu_t)=4t^2/(1+4t^2)`,
`sigma_t^2+Var(mu_t)=1` for all t.

Already at t=1, the actual mean variance is `(4/5)^2*(1+1/4)=4/5`, while Eq18 gives `4/25*(1+1)=8/25`. As t increases the actual mean variance tends to1, in place of the zero limit asserted in the proof. The schedule-independent invariant also disproves the claim for every arbitrarily small c>0 and its integer-rounded sample sizes; the choice c=1 only makes all sample counts literal integers. The mean-bias part of Theorem3 is not the source of the failure.

More generally the correct closed form is

`V_t=bar_sigma^2+(sigma0^2-bar_sigma^2)*product_(s=1)^t beta_s^2`.

This verifies that the defect concerns preservation of inherited uncertainty throughout the chain, rather than a single finite-sample approximation. The full paper and AppendixA impose no assumption that removes the shared hypothesis or excludes the positive-variance initial teacher used here.

**Reason for rejection.** Strong self-sustainability for a continuous Gaussian hypothesis space is a central standalone contribution, Theorem3, introduced specifically because the finite-hypothesis argument cannot handle that setting. The claimed growing-sample mechanism is supposed to eliminate the total uncertainty. In a fully admissible Gaussian instance it eliminates none of it: total variance is exactly its initial unit value for every session and every possible length schedule. A larger constant, a faster growth exponent, or a corrected proof cannot restore the theorem under the stated model. Repair requires changing how hypotheses are transmitted or withdrawing the strong concentration conclusion and its purported Gaussian extension. That loss of a main theoretical guarantee warrants rejection of the paper as written. This finding does not assert that its separate finite-hypothesis mean-preservation or network-consensus results are all false; deleting this guarantee would remove, rather than validate, the failed central contribution.

**Discovery method.** While tracing Eq18 from the sampling paragraph and Eq17, noticed that a session uses one shared random hypothesis, so its observations cannot be treated as unconditionally independent. Investigated whether the inherited covariance could vanish under the proposed length schedule.

**Verification method.** Read all28 pages and AppendixA; rechecked the model, definition, Eq17/Eq18 and Theorem3 on the original rendered PDF pages10–11. Re-derived the covariance and total-variance recursion from independent Gaussian variables and proved the unit-variance invariant by induction. Verified the exact first-step values and general closed form in1000 parameter-varied fixtures, a100000-session recurrence, and a100000-path Monte Carlo control of the written shared-h process. The analytic identity, not the simulation, establishes the asymptotic counterexample. Continued checking all remaining theorems; repeated uses of the same dependence error are not counted as separate issues.

 Completed controls: an unpublished audit file and `central-controls.log`, with marker `ITERATED539_ACTUAL_SUCCESS`, produced by an unpublished audit file. Full claim coverage and preserving repairs for other proof defects: an unpublished audit file. This is a theoretical finding; no missing experiment or unavailable source-code artifact is used as evidence.

Independent bounded QA re-read original rendered pages10–11 and checked100 exact rational recurrence steps: an unpublished audit file and `root-bounded-qa.json`. That QA confirmed the same missing covariance, legal parameters and invariant; it was not a second whole-paper review.

**Confidence.** High. The counterexample satisfies the exact sampling rule and all Gaussian assumptions, uses positive integer sample sizes, and contradicts the defined conclusion by an exact schedule-independent invariant. The first-step calculation independently exposes the missing covariance, and independent original-PDF/exact-arithmetic QA agrees. The result does not depend on numerical precision, a boundary case, or an unverified empirical attribution.

findings.title: The sparse model omits the probability cost of selecting a document-specific simplex face, invalidating its ELBO and competitive-perplexity evidence
findings.source_heading: ## Issue 2019__accepted__v20-18-569__I01 — The sparse model omits the probability cost of selecting a document-specific simplex face, invalidating its ELBO and competitive-perplexity evidence
findings.markdown:
**Exact location.** PDF7, Section4.2, the definition of the encoder-selected binary mask and degenerate `Dir(b·alpha)`, and Eq5–6; PDF10, Section4.3, the stated ordinary Dirichlet prior; PDF15, Sections5.4/5.5.1, the ELBO-based perplexity and claimed sparse-model advantage; Tables1/2/4/5 on PDF16/17/24/25; PDF22 conclusion. In the prepublication implementation, `nvdm_bernoulli.py` lines70–102 and196–200 compute the masked prior/posterior score. These are instances of one missing mask-probability term.

**Claim.** The encoder transforms each document into a positive concentration vector alpha and a rounded sigmoid mask b. The latent distribution is the degenerate Dirichlet on the selected sub-simplex. Eq5–6 calls the resulting reconstruction-minus-KL objective an ELBO for the generative model. Section4.3 states `p(z)=Dir(alpha0)`, with strictly positive prior concentrations. Section5.4 evaluates all models by ELBO-derived perplexity using analytical KL, and Section5.5.1 attributes the sparse model's lower, competitive perplexity to decoupling sparsity and smoothness. This decoupling with good likelihood is a central abstract/title/conclusion contribution.

**Error and evidence.** Let b select a nonempty proper face F of the topic simplex. The stipulated masked posterior has `q(F|x)=1`. An ordinary Dirichlet with positive concentrations has `p(F)=0`, including when its density diverges toward the boundary. Thus q is not absolutely continuous relative to the stated prior: `KL(q||p)=infinity`, not the finite regularizer used in the model. The literal ELBO is minus infinity for a sparse face.

The recovered original code does mask **both** distributions, so it does not directly evaluate that infinite full-Dirichlet KL. It computes a finite same-face divergence against `Dir_b(alpha0)`. But its chosen prior face is the encoder's document-dependent b(x). This conditional prior cannot be substituted for one unconditional generative prior without paying for face selection.

Here is an exact counterexample to treating that finite objective as an unconditional ELBO. Use two topics and two possible one-word documents A and B. Let `b(A)=(1,0)` and `b(B)=(0,1)`, and set alpha=alpha0 to any positive common vector, for example(.1,.1). The two masked posterior/prior pairs are identical point masses at e1 and e2, respectively, so both same-face KL values are0. Choose a legal categorical softmax decoder with `p(A|e1)=p(B|e2)=9/10` and cross probabilities1/10; logits(log9,0) and(0,log9) realize it. The alleged ELBO for each document is log(9/10). If both were lower bounds for a single normalized marginal, then `p(A)+p(B)>=9/10+9/10=9/5`, impossible. These are valid positive concentrations and nonempty binary masks; neither an all-zero mask nor a limiting numerical density is needed.

A native execution of the unchanged original NVDM class in TensorFlow1.13.1 corroborates the issue. With legal decoder weights, binary masks fed to the corresponding internal tensors and alpha=prior=(1,1), the original sampled and analytical KL operators both return0. Keeping the original decoder batch normalization, each of the two different documents receives exp(allegedELBO)=0.880710125, summing to1.76142025. The difference from the separate exact9/10 fixture comes from retaining batch normalization. Same-face KL=0 is also verified at all four published positive prior values(.02,.1,.3,.6). This is a controlled model/operator counterexample, not a claim to have recovered the historical trained weights.

**Rechecked model completion and material consequence.** A legitimate mixture prior `p(b,z)=pi(b)Dir_b(alpha0)` can repair the generative model. For deterministic b(x), however, its valid ELBO is the reported same-face score **plus log pi(b(x))**. Equivalently, KL includes the additional cost `-log pi(b(x))`. Different masks have disjoint relative-interior strata, so this term cannot be canceled by another Dirichlet normalization.

There is an explicit repair that leaves training unchanged: uniform pi over the `2^K-1` nonempty masks adds the constant `c_K=log(2^K-1)` per document to negative ELBO. This is compatible with independent Bernoulli probability.5 conditioned on a nonempty mask. It **does** preserve training gradients and topic coherence. It does **not** preserve the central likelihood/perplexity evidence: for D documents and N words, Sparse perplexity is multiplied by `exp(D*c_K/N)`.

The author's authenticated prepublication20news test file, processed by its original zero-document filtering, contains7,487 nonempty documents and629,312 words. The factors are approximately1.510322 for K50 and5.203289 for K200. Applying this deterministic correction to the printed20news scores gives:

| Prior | Topics | PDF/table | Reported Sparse | Uniform-mask correction | Reported ProdLDA |
|---|---:|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 0.02 | 50 | 16/1 | 1066 | 1610.00 | 1128 |
| 0.02 | 200 | 16/1 | 1075 | 5593.54 | 1271 |
| 0.1 | 50 | 17/2 | 1080 | 1631.15 | 1041 |
| 0.1 | 200 | 17/2 | 1100 | 5723.62 | 1294 |
| 0.3 | 50 | 24/4 | 1030 | 1555.63 | 1076 |
| 0.3 | 200 | 24/4 | 1123 | 5843.29 | 1496 |
| 0.6 | 50 | 25/5 | 954 | 1440.85 | 1139 |
| 0.6 | 200 | 25/5 | 971 | 5052.39 | 2104 |

All eight Sparse-versus-ProdLDA comparisons reverse under this explicit training-preserving model completion. The high-prior comparisons with dense DVAE reverse too: at prior.6/K200, Sparse971 becomes approximately5,053, versus dense DVAE1,035; at prior.3/K200, Sparse1,123 becomes approximately5,843, versus dense DVAE2,869. The exact values and factors are in the machine evidence. These calculations are conditional on the recovered author corpus and the stated uniform-mask completion. They are corrected printed-bound scores, not new trained models or true marginal likelihoods. A different nonuniform mask prior might yield other rankings, but the paper supplies neither those probabilities nor the corresponding valid evidence. No universal statement about every possible repaired prior is made.

**Reason for rejection.** The novel sparse architecture is presented as a probabilistic mechanism that decouples sparsity and smoothness while obtaining lower, competitive perplexity. Its stated full-Dirichlet ELBO is invalid; the finite implementation instead gives document-conditioned prior support for free. Consequently its likelihood comparisons do not establish the central claimed benefit. The most direct model completion can retain the training procedure, but it materially changes that evidence and reverses the documented comparisons above. Merely correcting a displayed symbol cannot retain the claim. A coherent mask prior and corrected likelihood evaluation, with the central conclusions reassessed, are necessary. This warrants rejection of the paper as written. The dense DVAE's topic-coherence contribution can remain; this finding does not claim to refute it.

**Discovery method.** While tracing the sparse posterior into the analytical Dirichlet KL, noticed that an encoder-created face is singular relative to the stated positive full-simplex prior. Inspection of the original code revealed its same-mask prior substitution. Investigated whether this resolved the model identity and whether the obvious constant-cost repair preserved the central empirical conclusion.

**Verification method.** Read all27pages, including AppendixA and every table/figure; rechecked original full rendered PDF7/10/11/14/15/16/17/22/24/25 and all five page contacts. Proved the support mismatch and exact two-document normalization contradiction. Verified original operators/full class in native TensorFlow1.13.1, at all four published priors. Independently derived the mixture-mask KL decomposition; counted the authenticated original test corpus with the original loader; read each compared value from the rendered tables; recomputed the correction. Independent bounded reviewer QA re-read the original decisive pages and reproduced the same-face calculation/counterexample, while explicitly challenging the training-preserving repair. Continued checking dense sampling, gradients, alternatives and empirical procedures afterward.

**Evidence and reproduction.** an unpublished audit file contains the exact certificate,30 analytical-versus-integrated ordinary Dirichlet KL checks, corpus hash/counts, all eight corrected comparisons and source hashes; helper completed55 checks. Native corpus coverage is five optimization batches on original20news data and one200-document test batch, not convergence or a table replay. `source-provenance.json` authenticates all11 Git blobs at author commit `d514d446dca5e46e318ecf7a162fbbc41769e028` (2019-07-31), in [the author's implementation](https://github.com/sophieburkhardt/dirichlet-vae-topic-models/tree/d514d446dca5e46e318ecf7a162fbbc41769e028).

**Confidence.** High for the error and its central scope: exact measure-support and finite-normalization proofs, original-PDF rechecks, authenticated original code, native operator corroboration and independent QA agree. The uniform-mask numerical consequences are deterministic given the recovered corpus and printed scores; historical training/table artifacts were not recovered, and alternative repaired priors were not evaluated. The severity assessment explicitly considers and acknowledges the training-preserving repair.

findings.title: The claimed full diagram density does not exist for the stated Gaussian pointcloud model
findings.source_heading: ## Issue 2019__accepted__v20-18-618__I01 — The claimed full diagram density does not exist for the stated Gaussian pointcloud model
findings.markdown:
**Exact location.** PDF page9, Definitions12–13, Eq3.5–3.7 and Remark14 (the reference measure and full global pdf); PDF page18, Section4.2, paragraph asserting A2/A3 for compact-set samples perturbed by Gaussian noise; PDF pages31–32, Example3 (ten noisy circle points and convergence to their true global pdf); PDF page36, Discussion (inheritance from underlying data and full-distribution/likelihood interpretation). The conditional convergence result to which these claims are connected is Theorem31, PDF19.

**Claim.** The global pdf consists of ordinary Lebesgue densities on all cardinality layers W^N, each of dimension2N for H1 birth/death pairs. The paper states that its bounded-density/tail assumptions hold for data sampled from a compact subset of Euclidean space and perturbed by Gaussian noise. Example3 expressly uses ten independent uniform unit-circle points with independent N(0,(1/50)^2 I2) errors, computes Cech degree-one diagrams, and describes KDE convergence to their true global pdf. This model has a smooth, everywhere-positive underlying point density. The claimed inheritance concerns the full diagram law, beyond its individual-feature intensity or low-cardinality slices.

**Error and evidence.** Smooth point noise does not make the full persistence-diagram law absolutely continuous: endpoints of different bars obey geometric dependencies. The following exact positive-probability configuration under the paper's own Example3 law proves that its required full pdf does not exist.

Take the ten rational planar points

`x_(i,j)=(i+j/2,87j/100), j=0,1,2,3, i=0,...,3-j`.

At Cech ball radius r=27/50=.54, their complex is a connected graph with10vertices,18edges and no triangles. All45pair and120triple enclosing radii can be checked exactly: the largest included edge radius squared is10069/40000<.53^2; the smallest excluded edge radius squared is30069/40000>.55^2; the smallest triple enclosing radius squared is101384761/302760000>.55^2. Thus H1 has dimension18-10+1=9 at r=.54. No higher-dimensional simplex can occur without a triangle.

The minimum-enclosing-ball radius is1-Lipschitz in the maximum per-point displacement. Therefore moving each point by less than.001 preserves this graph and its nine holes at.54. This is an open event, not a zero-probability exact lattice. The Example3 circle-plus-Gaussian density is strictly positive throughout the plane, so the product of these ten small disks has strictly positive probability under its exact iid sampling law. Every diagram in the event has **at least nine** positive finite H1 bars. The total number of bars is bounded by the finite number of edges, so at least one finite cardinality N>=9 has positive probability on this event.

Now remove translation and rotation from an arbitrary ten-point configuration: set its first point to0 and its second on a positive axis. Only17real shape coordinates remain. Cech H1 births are chosen from edge half-distances; deaths are chosen from triple enclosing radii, either half a longest edge or an acute-triangle circumradius. Away from coincidences/collinearities (probability0 here), these are finitely many analytic functions on countably many locally Lipschitz charts of those17coordinates. Consequently an ordered N-bar endpoint vector is in a finite/countable union of images of17dimensional charts in R^(2N). For N>=9, 2N>=18>17, so each such image has2N-dimensional Lebesgue measure0. Finite endpoint selections and feature permutations preserve this nullity; the1/N! convention in Eq3.5 cannot change it.

Combining the two steps, some N>=9 layer assigns positive probability to a Lebesgue-null subset. Hence the **actual Example3 full diagram law has no global pdf in the paper's Definition13 sense**. It cannot satisfy A2/A3, and ordinary KDE cannot converge to a full target pdf that does not exist. Smoothness or tail decay of the underlying Gaussian density does not remove this dependence.

There is also a direct five-bar dependence near the compact pointcloud consisting of center(0,0) and outer vertices(1,0),(.3,.95),(-.8,.6),(-.8,-.6),(.3,-.95). Exact rational checks show five acute fan triangles with strictly empty circumcircles and outer-edge births. These properties hold on an open neighborhood. If b_i,d_i are its five positive-bar endpoints, the law of sines and the central angles winding around the center give the symmetric identity

`sum_(i=1)^5 arcsin(b_i/d_i)=2pi`.

It defines a9dimensional hypersurface in the10dimensional five-bar layer. Under independent Gaussian jitter around this fixed compact pointcloud, the probability of this singular event approaches1 as noise decreases. The issue therefore can dominate in the general Gaussian-perturbed pointcloud setting, in addition to the positive-probability counterexample in the exact iid Example3.

**Scope of the demonstrated failure.** This counterexample does **not** disprove Theorem31 when one separately assumes an existing suitable full density. It disproves the paper's express inheritance/applicability claim for its intended pointcloud models and its true-global-pdf interpretation of Example3. Some low-cardinality slices, intensity/PHD estimates, finite-bandwidth smooth surrogates and bottleneck moment estimates can remain meaningful. Weak convergence of smoothed measures to a singular law is a different conclusion from convergence to its ordinary full joint density.

**Reason for rejection.** The paper's central advance is a consistent estimator of the **full joint distribution density** of random persistence diagrams, distinguished from the already available individual-feature/PHD approaches, with applicability and likelihood interpretation justified for Gaussian-noisy pointclouds. In its explicit validation model, the target full density does not exist; the claimed assumptions do not follow from the stipulated noise. Numerical low-dimensional slices cannot establish the missing full-law result. Repair requires a singular/stratified reference measure and new estimation theory, or withdrawing the claimed noisy-pointcloud application and full-density interpretation of a principal experiment. Adding more samples, a continuity condition, a bandwidth adjustment or an extra tail bound cannot make these singular layers absolutely continuous. This loss of the central full-law applicability and validation warrants rejection of the paper as written, even though conditional density-class theory and moment/intensity contributions may survive.

**Discovery method.** While tracing the claimed inheritance of a full diagram density from Gaussian point noise, noticed that many barcode endpoints depend on the same small set of geometric coordinates. Investigated whether an actual open set could contain more birth/death coordinates than shape parameters, rather than relying on a degenerate configuration.

**Verification method.** Read all49pages including both appendices, then rechecked the definitions, assumption claim, exact Example3 conditions and discussion on original rendered pages9/18/19/31/36. Constructed and verified all45pair/120triple inequalities using exact rational arithmetic; proved the open-event probability and17-versus2N dimension argument. Independently computed full Cech2skeleton persistence on200 nearby ten-point configurations and200 pentagonal configurations. A separate native GUDHI3.11.0 exact AlphaComplex computation matched100 configurations of each type to2.23e-16. Verified the five-bar law-of-sines relation and its open-neighborhood geometry. The analytic null-set proof establishes nonexistence; simulations only crosscheck the filtration. Continued reviewing all remaining results and experiments. Independent bounded root QA re-read the decisive original pages and separately verified the exact geometric certificate and dimension argument.

 Exact rational certificate and Cech controls: an unpublished audit file, produced by an unpublished audit file; its successful execution log is an unpublished audit file (marker `PERSISTENCE618_GEOMETRY_ACTUAL_SUCCESS`). Independent native controls: an unpublished audit file and `secondary-controls.log`, produced by an unpublished audit file (marker `PERSISTENCE618_SECONDARY_ACTUAL_SUCCESS`). OriginalPDF integrity: an unpublished audit file. No unavailable author artifact or failed empirical rerun is used as proof of this mathematical finding.

**Confidence.** High. The primary counterexample satisfies the exact Example3 iid sampling model on an open event of positive probability. Exact rational inequalities establish nine live holes, and the dimension obstruction establishes positive singular mass without numerical rank estimates. Original definitions explicitly use full2N-dimensional Lebesgue layers, and independent exact-arithmetic/original-PDF QA agrees. The severity assessment concerns the paper's central promised data model and full-density validation; the conditional theorem distinction is explicit.

In its explicit validation model, the target full density does not exist; the claimed assumptions do not follow from the stipulated noise. Numerical low-dimensional slices cannot establish the missing full-law result. Repair requires a singular/stratified reference measure and new estimation theory, or withdrawing the claimed noisy-pointcloud application and full-density interpretation of a principal experiment. Adding more samples, a continuity condition, a bandwidth adjustment or an extra tail bound cannot make these singular layers absolutely continuous. This loss of the central full-law applicability and validation warrants rejection of the paper as written, even though conditional density-class theory and moment/intensity contributions may survive.

findings.title: The advertised higher-order smoothing accuracy is false: converged estimates have ordinary Laplace error
findings.source_heading: ## Issue 2019__accepted__v20-18-659__I01 — The advertised higher-order smoothing accuracy is false: converged estimates have ordinary Laplace error
findings.markdown:
**Exact location.** PDF pages23–24, AppendixA, especially Eq27 and the conclusion `lambda_hat−lambda_hat_star=O(n^-3)` on page24. PDF page21, Discussion, repeats this as the method's theoretical high-accuracy guarantee. PDF pages9–10, Eq22–25, specify the approximate-EM score and closed-form smoothing update; PDF page6, Eq12, defines the ordinary Laplace log-marginal approximation used for comparison.

**Claim.** AppendixA asserts that the learned smoothing hyperparameters differ from their exact marginal-likelihood maximizers by O(n^-3) for the proposed double-Laplace method, improving on the O(n^-2) error asserted for ordinary Laplace. It assumes a twice continuously differentiable log-marginal with an invertible Hessian throughout an open convex neighborhood of the maximizer, and derives the extra order by treating hyperparameter curvature as order n. The Discussion expressly presents the O(n^-3) smoothing-parameter error as a theoretical accuracy advantage. This concerns the converged hyperparameters, beyond an approximation to a single moment or objective value.

**Error and evidence.** The printed update has exactly the **ordinary single-Laplace stationary points**. Its claimed additional order fails in an explicit smooth, identifiable, single-mode GAM satisfying the paper's centering and integrated-roughness assumptions.

First write the ordinary Laplace objective, up to constants, as

`L*(lambda)=.5 log|S_lambda|_+ + lP(w_lambda;lambda) − .5 log det H_lambda`.

The mode satisfies `dw_lambda/dlambda_j=−H_lambda^-1 S_j w_lambda` (the paper's Eq22). Differentiating L* gives

`dL*/dlambda_j=.5[rank(S_j)/lambda_j − w_lambda^T S_j w_lambda − tr{H_lambda^-1(S_j+dH_L/dlambda_j)}]`.

This is precisely `G_j(lambda;lambda)` in Eq24. Therefore an interior fixed point of Eq25 solves the ordinary Laplace score. Calling its iteration a double-Laplace E-step cannot supply a different higher-accuracy converged solution.

For a concrete counterexample, let n=2m and use an exponential-rate GAM with an unpenalized intercept a and one smooth coefficient w:

`Y_i independently follows Exponential(rate exp(a+w*b(t_i)))`.

Take m inputs at t=0 and m at t=2, and use the twice differentiable basis

`b(t)=t^2/2−1, 0<=t<=2`.

The observed basis values are −1 and +1 in equal numbers, so the required sum-to-zero constraint holds exactly. Its integrated squared second derivative is `S=integral_0^2 (b''(t))^2 dt=2`. Thus the penalty is `.5*(2lambda)*w^2`; put `kappa=2lambda`. The smoothing parameter is positive and the intercept has the allowed flat prior. Set the two positive observation sums to `B_minus=m*exp(1)` and `B_plus=m*exp(−1)`. All observations can be positive, for example equal to their corresponding group averages.

The log-likelihood is, up to a data constant,

`lL(a,w)=n*a − n*exp(a)*cosh(w−1)`.

It is smooth and strictly concave in the identifiable two-dimensional regression vector. Adding the positive quadratic smooth penalty preserves a unique finite mode with a positive definite Hessian. Integrating the flat intercept is exact:

`integral_R exp[n*a − n*exp(a)*cosh(w−1)] da = Gamma(n)/[n*cosh(w−1)]^n`.

Consequently the exact remaining posterior in w is proportional to

`exp{−n*log cosh(w−1) − kappa*w^2/2}`.

This posterior and the marginal likelihood are finite. At the joint mode, `a=−log cosh(w−1)` and

`det H_joint = n*[n*sech^2(w−1)+kappa]`.

Hence the ordinary two-dimensional Laplace marginal objective equals the one-dimensional Laplace objective of this **exactly intercept-integrated** model, up to a kappa-independent constant. Its stationary point is the proposed method's converged solution by the preceding score identity.

Let `g(w)=−n*log cosh(w−1)−kappa*w^2/2`, and let H=−g'' at its mode. Uniformly for kappa near1, the mode and derivatives satisfy

`w=1−kappa/n+O(n^-2)`,
`H=n+kappa+O(n^-1)`,
`g'''=−2kappa+O(n^-1)`,
`g''''=2n+O(n^-1)`.

The first Laplace log-integral correction is

`C1=g''''/(8H^2)+5(g''')^2/(24H^3)=1/(4n)−kappa/(2n^2)+O(n^-3)`.

The further order-n^-2 log-correction has a kappa-independent leading coefficient: at leading order the standardized likelihood derivatives at w=1 contain no kappa. Its derivative is therefore O(n^-3). It follows that

`L_exact'(kappa)−L*'(kappa)=−1/(2n^2)+O(n^-3)`.

Both interior maximizers tend to kappa=1, and `L*''(kappa)→−1/2`, rather than growing as n. Taylor expansion of the score at the maximizers therefore gives

`kappa_exact−kappa_method=−1/n^2+O(n^-3)`,

or, in the paper's actual smoothing coordinate,

**`lambda_exact−lambda_method=−1/(2n^2)+O(n^-3)`**.

The nonzero n^-2 coefficient contradicts the claimed O(n^-3) error. All the appendix's stated local differentiability and invertible-Hessian assumptions hold. The unsupported step is treating the marginal Hessian in a smoothing hyperparameter as if it were the order-n regression-parameter information matrix; the two matrices have different scaling here.

This is also a counterexample in the usual probabilistic asymptotic regime, without requiring exactly repeated continuous observations. With arbitrary positive group sums,

`B_minus*exp(−w)+B_plus*exp(w)=2sqrt(B_minus*B_plus)*cosh(w−a_n)`,
`a_n=.5 log(B_minus/B_plus)`.

For independent observations from the same model with a=0,w=1, the strong law gives a_n→1 almost surely. The expansion is uniform for a_n near1, so the same nonzero n^-2 error persists for typical data. The displayed deterministic sums simply make every formula transparent.

As a numerical crosscheck, independent60-digit integrations and root solves at n=20,40,80,160,320,640 give n² times the paper-coordinate error −.524367,−.508142,−.503074,−.501289,−.500583,−.500276, approaching the exact coefficient −1/2. The original two-dimensional Eq24 score agrees with the ordinary Laplace score to below1e-50. These checks corroborate the analytic expansion; numerical extrapolation is not the proof.

**Reason for rejection.** A central theoretical advantage claimed for the proposed optimization is higher-order accuracy in the learned smoothing parameters, justified by the double-Laplace construction and AppendixA. The algorithm actually converges to the same single-Laplace stationary point, and a fully regular GAM has the ordinary n^-2 error with an explicit nonzero coefficient. A proof clarification, convergence tolerance or extra data cannot deliver the advertised n^-3 guarantee. Retaining it requires changing the approximation/estimator; retaining the current estimator requires withdrawing this substantive theoretical accuracy advantage and its stated justification. That loss warrants rejection of the paper as written. This finding does not claim that the implementation cannot be fast or empirically useful, or that every reported comparison is false.

**Discovery method.** While tracing AppendixA, noticed that its order-n curvature assertion concerned smoothing hyperparameters, whose marginal likelihood need not accumulate order-n information. Differentiating the actual update also revealed that its diagonal score equals the ordinary Laplace score, motivating an exact marginal-likelihood comparison.

**Verification method.** Read all27pages and AppendixA, and inspected original full renders9/10/21/23/24 to establish the exact claimed quantity and equations. Re-derived the general score identity and constructed the centered quadratic-basis GAM with its real roughness penalty and unpenalized intercept. Integrated the intercept analytically, checked identifiability/propriety/local curvature, and derived the nonzero n^-2 optimum error. Performed60-digit posterior integrations/root solves and independently evaluated the original two-dimensional score. Reviewed the cited Tierney etal1989 primary paper's rendered pages710–713 to check the approximation's scope. Independent bounded root QA re-read the original claims, re-derived the joint integration/determinant/asymptotics and corroborated the result with separate SciPy quadrature/root computations. Continued checking the remaining claims and all experiments; lower-threshold defects are recorded privately rather than added as qualifying findings.

 Actual centered-GAM controls: an unpublished audit file and `.log`, helper (marker `SMOOTH659_GAM_ASYMPTOTIC_ACTUAL_SUCCESS`). Independent scalar/score controls: an unpublished audit file and `.log`, helper. All mathematical evidence is tied to the original PDF; postpublication author code is only corroborating evidence, and no unavailable original rerun establishes this finding.

**Confidence.** High. The score identity is exact, the counterexample meets the actual GAM centering/roughness/intercept assumptions, and exact intercept integration reduces it to a regular one-dimensional asymptotic calculation with nonzero n^-2 coefficient. Independent original-PDF, analytic and numerical QA agrees. Finite quadrature is corroboration; the analytic argument and typical-data extension establish the contradicted rate.

findings.title: The general low-energy guarantee is false: some bounded continuous targets cannot attain its claimed risk at any parameter
findings.source_heading: ## Issue 2019__accepted__v20-18-674__I01 — The general low-energy guarantee is false: some bounded continuous targets cannot attain its claimed risk at any parameter
findings.markdown:
**Exact location.** PDF page13, Theorem16(1), with the square-integrable-data setting on page12 and the bias convention in Remark17 on page13. PDF page29, AppendixC, opening inference from RKHS density to an L2 feature-density representation and subsequent application of Bach2017b Proposition1. The near-inverse-width energy guarantee is also advertised among the contributions on PDF pages1–2.

**Claim.** Section5 considers square-integrable X,Y and a positively homogeneous activation. Theorem16(1) asserts that, after uniformly sampling the initial first-layer weights, with probability at least1−delta there is a non-increasing-loss path to risk at most `R(X,Y)+lambda` once

`p >= C*lambda^-1*log(1/(lambda*delta))`.

Here C is a finite constant independent of lambda,delta,p for the fixed data model, and `R(X,Y)=E|Y−E[Y|X]|^2` is the Bayes risk. Unlike part2, part1 states no regularity or finite-RKHS-norm condition on the regression target. Remark17 expressly includes biases by augmenting the input and states that this convention applies to this theorem.

**Error and evidence.** Density of an RKHS in L2 does not mean that an arbitrary target belongs to that RKHS or has a bounded feature-density norm. The claimed rate fails even for the best width-p ReLU network with freely trainable weights and biases. The following is one fixed probability distribution and one bounded target that extends continuously to the compact input interval.

For each integer k>=1, set

`M_k=16^k, N_k=3M_k, q_k=2^-k, a_k=2^-k`,
`I_k=(2^-k, 2^-k+2^(-k-2))`,
`x_(k,j)=2^-k + j*2^(-k-2)/(3M_k+1), j=1,...,3M_k`.

These are equally spaced points in mutually disjoint intervals. Give each point probability `q_k/(3M_k)`. The probabilities sum to1 because `sum_(k>=1) q_k=1`. In each block let the deterministic responses repeat the triples

`(a_k,−a_k,a_k)`.

Thus 0<X<1 and |Y|<=1/2, so both variables are square integrable; the Bayes risk is0. The regression target is continuous on the support including its only accumulation point0: set its value at0 to0, interpolate linearly between successive atoms and across gaps, and extend outside the extreme atoms. Since a_k→0, this gives a bounded continuous extension on[0,1]. The activation is ReLU, which satisfies the theorem's positive homogeneity and integrability conditions.

Any scalar width-p one-hidden-layer ReLU network with biases is a continuous piecewise affine function with at most p breakpoints. This remains true if an extra affine output term is allowed, so the following bound applies to a class at least as expressive as the paper's model.

Partition block k into its M_k disjoint triples. At most p of the open intervals from the first to the third point of a triple contain a breakpoint. On every other triple the network is affine. For any equally spaced triple, the vector `(1,−2,1)` annihilates affine values and has squared norm6. Its inner product with `(a_k,−a_k,a_k)` is4a_k, so Cauchy–Schwarz gives the exact residual bound

`sum_(three points) (network−target)^2 >= (4a_k)^2/6 = 8a_k^2/3`.

Therefore, for **every** width-p network,

`L(theta) >= [q_k/(3M_k)]*(M_k−p)*(8a_k^2/3)`
`          = (8/9)*q_k*a_k^2*(1−p/M_k)`

when p<=M_k. In particular, choose `p_k=M_k/2=16^k/2`. Then

**`inf_theta L(theta) >= 4/(9*8^k)`**.

Now take `lambda_k=1/(10*8^k)` and fix delta=1/2. The theorem's required width, apart from its fixed constant C, is

`lambda_k^-1*log(1/(lambda_k*delta)) = 10*8^k*(k*log8+log20)`.

But

`p_k/[lambda_k^-1*log(1/(lambda_k*delta))]`
`=2^(k−1)/[10*(k*log8+log20)] -> infinity`.

For every finite constant C allowed by the theorem, sufficiently large k therefore satisfies its width requirement, while every possible endpoint has

`L(theta) >= 4/(9*8^k) = (40/9)*lambda_k > R(X,Y)+lambda_k`.

There is no parameter attaining the promised risk, so no such path exists for **any** initialization. The event claimed to have probability at least1/2 actually has probability0 on this subsequence. This is a fixed-data-model asymptotic counterexample, rather than a new distribution chosen for each network width, or a failure confined to fixed random features.

The unsupported proof step is explicit on PDF29: from density of H in L2, the authors assume without loss of generality `f*=Tg*` with `g* in L2(dτ)`. For these unit augmented ReLU features, every such representation is Lipschitz:

`|Tg(x)−Tg(y)| <= ||g||_L2(dτ)*|x−y|`.

The constructed target has adjacent-atom slopes

`2a_k/[2^(-k-2)/(3*16^k+1)] = 8*(3*16^k+1) -> infinity`.

It therefore cannot have the asserted finite-norm representation, even on the input support. Approximating it by members of the dense RKHS cannot preserve a constant independent of the target accuracy when those norms diverge. The cited Bach2017b Proposition1 is explicitly an approximation bound for the **unit ball of the RKHS**, not arbitrary L2 functions; original reference PDF page16 confirms this restriction.

**Scope checked against the original paper.** PDF12 motivates random features with a conditional integral-representation discussion, and the proof sketch introduces a density. Neither supplies a standing finite-RKHS-norm assumption in Theorem16(1); the appendix instead tries to obtain that representation from density for the stated square-integrable-data setting. The counterexample pinpoints why that reduction fails. Part2 explicitly assumes a bounded representation density; that separate restricted result is not refuted here. The lower bound establishes the failure of the promised Bayes-risk threshold; it does not, by itself, claim that the constructed loss has a spurious valley, nor that the finite-dimensional or worst-case-valley theorems are all false.

**Reason for rejection.** The general, near-inverse-width low-energy guarantee is a central standalone contribution: it is meant to explain why the paper's worst-case bad valleys become harmless with high probability as the width grows. Under its stated data assumptions the guaranteed energy is sometimes unattainable even by a globally optimized network, with no initialization or optimization obstacle involved. No proof clarification, logarithmic factor or larger fixed width constant repairs the rate. A valid result needs a substantive target-complexity/RKHS-norm restriction or a slower target-dependent approximation term, withdrawing the advertised general square-integrable-data conclusion. That loss of a main theoretical guarantee warrants rejection of the paper as written. Other landscape results and the explicitly regular part2 may remain useful.

**Discovery method.** While tracing the random-feature argument, noticed that AppendixC replaces density of the RKHS by exact membership before applying a norm-restricted approximation theorem. Investigated whether the rate could fail for the whole trainable network class, rather than only for its particular proof or fixed features.

**Verification method.** Read all34pages and AppendicesA–E. Rechecked the exact assumptions, theorem, bias convention and proof on original rendered pages12/13/28/29, and read the cited Bach Proposition1 on its original rendered PDF page16. Constructed the fixed compact atomic distribution and continuous bounded target; verified its total probability, moments and ReLU model assumptions. Derived the exact affine-triple residual and breakpoint counting bound, then proved the width/tolerance contradiction for every finite constant. Checked100 exact rational block certificates and240 independent finite ReLU examples as computational controls; these finite checks corroborate the symbolic infinite-distribution proof. Continued checking all other central claims and appendices. Independent bounded root QA re-read the decisive original pages and separately verified the exact triple argument, fixed distribution and asymptotic contradiction; it was not a second whole-paper review.

 Completed controls: an unpublished audit file, helper; successful log (marker `VALLEYS674_ACTUAL_SUCCESS`). Other-claim checks and screened candidates: an unpublished audit file, helper, successful log. Primary-reference details and original page16: an unpublished audit file, `Bach2017-primary-page16.txt` and `.png`. This is a purely theoretical paper; no missing experiment or author-code artifact is used as error evidence.

**Confidence.** High. The target and probability distribution satisfy the stated assumptions, and an exact lower bound applies to every parameter and every initialization. The proof uses a count of ReLU breakpoints and an exact three-point least-squares residual, avoiding unverified optimization, numerical rank or asymptotic simulation. Original definitions and the cited norm-restricted source agree with the identified proof failure.
